panels.title: Engagement score — reactions + 5× comments (tier splits not collected yet)
Engagement score (latest month)

targets.rawSql: select scope::text as scope, score from dash.feed_page_engagement_score_totals where scope = 'last_week' order by ord

panels.description: The feed’s “last_week” scope is filled from the LATEST MONTH of the page export (the aggregate fallback in build-page-stats.mjs) — the company page publishes no weekly granularity, so this is a month, not a week. The newest month is PARTIAL: monthly.json was generated 2026-08-20, so 2026-08 covers about 20 days against 31 — it is NOT comparable to the full months beside it, and a drop in the last point or bar may be nothing but the missing days. If per-person collection later puts engagement.json in place, this scope becomes a real ISO week; this generator reads whether that file exists and words the title accordingly. Flat weighting only — reaction ×1, comment ×5. The ICP ×2 and VIP ×4 multipliers in scoring.json cannot be applied until per-person engagers are collected, which is why every tier panel here reads “???”. This number says nothing about WHO engaged.

panels.title: Engagement score (last 6 months)

targets.rawSql: select scope::text as scope, score from dash.feed_page_engagement_score_totals where scope = 'all_time' order by ord

panels.description: NOT a lifetime total. The page export is a rolling 6-month window (scrape-page.mjs --months=6) and monthly.json is OVERWRITTEN whole on every run, so months older than six are retained nowhere in this repo. This figure drops its oldest month on the next collection and can FALL while engagement rises. Flat weighting only — reaction ×1, comment ×5. The ICP ×2 and VIP ×4 multipliers in scoring.json cannot be applied until per-person engagers are collected, which is why every tier panel here reads “???”. This number says nothing about WHO engaged.

panels.title: Followers (reconstructed)

targets.rawSql: select week::text as week, followers from dash.feed_page_account_weeks order by ord

panels.description: NOT a measured history. The curve is computed BACKWARDS from the hand-entered current total (manual.json total_followers = 1362, recorded 2026-08-20) by subtracting each month’s new followers, so it ignores unfollows and can only ever slope upward — it could not show a decline even if the page lost followers every month. Only the newest point is a measured number, and it is exactly as stale as manual.json.

panels.title: Page visitors (monthly)

targets.rawSql: select week::text as week, unique_visitors from dash.feed_page_account_weeks order by ord

panels.description: LinkedIn’s Page metric “unique visitors”: a SUM OF DAILY UNIQUES over the month — one person who visits on three days counts three times. It is NOT a personal profile’s “profile viewers”, which counts distinct members over a rolling 90 days. Different object, different window, different definition. The newest month is PARTIAL: monthly.json was generated 2026-08-20, so 2026-08 covers about 20 days against 31 — it is NOT comparable to the full months beside it, and a drop in the last point or bar may be nothing but the missing days.

panels.title: Seniority — follower base (top 8)

targets.rawSql: select audience::text as audience, category::text as category, name::text as name, value from dash.feed_page_demographics where audience = 'followers' and category = 'Seniority' order by ord

panels.description: A snapshot of the CURRENT follower base — a headcount, top 8 rows of the export. The demographic sheets are a single snapshot over the LAST 365 DAYS (the export range scrape-page.mjs sets) — twice the 6-month window every other panel on this board shows. LinkedIn publishes no per-month demographic breakdown, so this is one slice, not a series.

panels.title: Seniority — page views by visitor seniority (12 mo, top 8)

targets.rawSql: select audience::text as audience, category::text as category, name::text as name, value from dash.feed_page_demographics where audience = 'visitors' and category = 'Seniority' order by ord

panels.description: Counts of page-VIEW events, not distinct people: one person visiting ten times counts ten, and the totals here run well above the page’s unique-visitor count. Top 8 rows of the export. The demographic sheets are a single snapshot over the LAST 365 DAYS (the export range scrape-page.mjs sets) — twice the 6-month window every other panel on this board shows. LinkedIn publishes no per-month demographic breakdown, so this is one slice, not a series. Comparable with the follower panel beside it in COMPOSITION only — never as a headcount, since the two are different units over the same 12 months.

panels.title: ICP geography — US vs India (company-page extra)
US · ICP share of visitor locations (6 mo)

targets.rawSql: select audience::text as audience, icp_pct from dash.feed_page_geo_aggregate where audience = 'visitors' order by ord

panels.description: Counts from the Visitors export’s Location sheet (only members whose location LinkedIn names), classified into ICP buckets by geo-monthly.py. Read these as COMPOSITION — the sheet is not a count of visitors. Across 2026-03–2026-08 it totals 2201, against 1681 unique visitors and 3890 page views over the same months — it matches neither, so it cannot be read as "how many people looked at the page".

panels.title: US · ICP share — followers (geo-classified subset)

targets.rawSql: select audience::text as audience, icp_pct from dash.feed_page_geo_aggregate where audience = 'followers' order by ord

panels.description: Computed over ONLY those followers whose country the export names — NOT over the follower base shown above. Unclassified followers are excluded from both the numerator and the denominator, so this percentage is an upper bound on the share of the real base. As recorded in manual.json, recorded 2026-08-20: 837 of 1362 followers are geo-classified, so 525 are invisible here; the US share of the FULL base is at most 356/1362 = 26.1%.
